newsitem.title: UK: British foreign minister attacks "corrupt" Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: British foreign minister attacks "corrupt" Nigeria.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Robin Cook launched a stinging attack on Nigeria on Wednesday, accusing its military government of corruption and saying it should remain suspended from the Commonwealth.

Cook's forthright comments, much stronger than those made by his Conservative predecessor on Nigeria, follow the new Labour government's announcement that it will put human rights at the centre of its foreign policy.
They were also a slap in the face for the powerful oil-producing west African nation, which last month urged Labour not to damage what it called the "special relationship" with Britain.

Nigeria, widely accused of human rights abuses, was suspended from the Commonwealth in November 1995 for executing writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight minority rights activists despite widespread appeals for clemency.
"Nigeria is a very interesting example of the way in which economic progress and human rights are complementary," Cook told reporters on Wednesday.
"Nigeria should not be a poor country: it has huge natural reserves and has every potential to be one of the two most wealthy countries in Africa.
"What holds it back is a corrupt regime and very poor standards of democratic government."

Shortly after taking power last month Cook said the world should be prepared to apply sanctions against Nigeria until it returned to the democratic fold. In 1993 the government overturned a presidential election and imprisoned the man presumed to have won.
Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha has been promising for some time to implement a two-year plan to restore democracy but critics say this is just a ruse to prolong his rule.

An eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG), trying for the last 18 months to work out how to deal with Nigeria, has been hampered by splits between member states on the best approach.

But Cook made it clear that he backed CMAG members such as Canada, which has long called for a tough response. CMAG is due to report to a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) at the end of October.
"Very significant progress has to be made towards democratic government and human rights before the suspension from the Commonwealth can be lifted," Cook said.
"Nothing has happened in Nigeria to justify the lifting of the suspension and I hope they (CMAG) would recommend that to CHOGM."

Last year CMAG recommended a package of sanctions -- including a ban on fresh arms sales and restriction of visas for senior officials -- be imposed on Nigeria but decided to suspend them to allow more time to investigate the situation in the country.

CMAG will hold a London meeting on July 10 and 11 to gather opinions from various Nigerian groups and will meet once more in September to finalise their position before the CHOGM meeting in Edinburgh.

Nigerian opposition activists consider CMAG's proposed sanctions to be ineffective and have always blamed Britain, the former colonial power, for not leading its western partners to take a tougher line.
The previous Conservative administration never fully backed the idea of sanctions, saying a punitive approach could hurt ordinary Nigerians rather than those in power.
Earlier this month the European Union extended for a further six months restrictions on contacts with Nigerian officials, saying not enough progress had been made to end human rights abuses.
